_help: Edit this file to change the site tour. 'cases' names the example decisions (found by citation, with the id as a fallback). Each step has: id, section, url (a page of the site; {name} is replaced by a case id from 'cases'), title, text, target (CSS selector or list of selectors tried in order; leave out to show the card in the middle of the screen), before (actions run once the page is ready: type, check, uncheck, click, submit, hover, waitFor, scroll; add 'unless' to skip an action when that selector is visible), buttons (extra buttons on the card; each says what it writes), hover (true: show the site's own hover card on the target), optional (true: skip silently when the target is missing, which is also what happens to any step whose target cannot be found), timeout (seconds to wait for the target, default 8), needs (a note for editors: the feature this step depends on). Actions also take: match (pick the visible element whose text matches), when (only act if that selector is visible), fill (paste a text from 'texts'), wait (ms). target can be {"css":...,"text":...}. fresh: reload when stepping back to it. writes: shown on the card when a step changes anything. needsData: the check script reports the step if its target is empty. 'probes' are searches the check script runs to confirm the example data exists. The tour signs in to the Workbench demo when it starts, and one step pins Vavilov to that demo list; nothing else is written.

fc.label: a recent Federal Court decision that cites Vavilov

texts.moa:
MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

steps.title: Welcome to iLit
steps.text: This is a short walk through the real site, using real decisions. I will open pages and run searches for you. Use Next and Back to move, Skip section to jump ahead, or Exit at any time. Nothing is saved or changed unless a step says so.

steps.title: Four places to work
steps.text: Case search is where you find and read decisions. Intelligence / Statistics adds up many decisions: judges, citations and Federal Court activity. Workbench is your own list of files and pinned decisions. Everything runs without AI, on stored data.

steps.title: Search by name or citation
steps.text: Type a case name or a citation such as 2019 SCC 65. Suggestions appear as you type. Let me search for the Supreme Court's leading decision on standard of review.

steps.title: A real search
steps.text: I searched for Vavilov. Each result shows the court, date, how the decision came out, and how many decisions cite it. Click a result to read it; I will open one in a moment.

steps.title: Search in a plain sentence
steps.text: I ticked 'Search the full decision text' and typed a plain sentence: the officer failed to consider the best interests of the child. Results are the decisions whose text matches. Avoid the word 'not' in a search: it is read as the NOT operator.
steps.needs: Paragraph search path (PR 373, merged). Works on the current site but is faster once deployed.

before.text: the officer failed to consider the best interests of the child

steps.title: Now something specific
steps.text: Say you want refugee cessation cases involving India. I ticked full-text search and searched for India. That finds every decision that mentions it, which is far too many, so the next two steps narrow it.

steps.title: Narrow by case type
steps.text: The Case type list in the filters groups decisions by type, worked out from the statute provisions each one discusses (no AI), with counts beside each. I opened Refugee protection and ticked Refugee cessation (s. 108), so only cessation cases that mention India remain.
steps.needs: Case type chips (merged to main; check deployed).

steps.title: Where the Minister won
steps.text: The outcome filter keeps decisions that went the government's way. I picked Government won. Filters combine: full text, case type and outcome together.

steps.title: The matching decisions
steps.text: These are the decisions where the Minister prevailed in India cessation matters. Each row shows the court, date, judge, outcome, case type and how many decisions cite it. Click a row to read it.

steps.title: The formatted reader
steps.text: This is Vavilov, formatted as a clean document with numbered paragraphs. The header shows the court, date, citation and how many decisions cite it, cite this, and refer to statutes.

steps.title: Outcome, details and topics
steps.text: The left panel gives the recorded outcome, the case details and the topics found in the text. The decision stays lit beside it: nothing is hidden or blocked.

steps.title: The Outline
steps.text: The Outline lists the decision's sections with their paragraph numbers. I jumped to one so you can see the text move; click any row to go there, or scroll the text yourself.

steps.title: Citations, statutes and tags in the text
steps.text: Citations (gold), statutes (purple) and topic tags (green) are marked in the text. Switch each layer on or off to read the decision clean or fully annotated.

steps.title: Hover a citation
steps.text: Hover a marked citation and a card shows what it is and the passage it points to. This is the card for one of the authorities this decision relies on.

steps.title: Hover a statute
steps.text: The same works for statutes and regulations. The card names the provision, and the left panel can show every decision that cites it.

steps.title: Authorities
steps.text: The Authorities tab lists the cases and statutes this decision cites, how often and at which paragraphs. The decision text stays live beside it.

steps.title: Jump through the decision by authority
steps.text: Find takes you to where an authority is cited in the text. I pressed it for the first case in the list: the passage is highlighted in the decision. Press it again to go to the next place it is cited; the text is yours to scroll.

steps.title: Intelligence for this decision
steps.text: The Intelligence tab adds the picture around this decision: the judge, how the decision has been cited, and links to the wider citation analysis.

steps.title: Keep it on your Workbench
steps.text: Save to Workbench pins a decision to your own list. I saved Vavilov for you, so it will appear on the Workbench in a moment.
steps.writes: This step pinned Vavilov to the demo Workbench list called Demo analyst. Remove it any time from the Workbench.

steps.title: A Federal Court decision
steps.text: Here is a recent Federal Court decision that cites Vavilov. Federal Court reasons open the same way: header, outcome, outline, and the authorities it applies.

steps.title: Other landmark decisions
steps.text: Baker (humanitarian and compassionate decisions), Dunsmuir (standards of review) and Khosa (Federal Courts Act judicial review) are all in the library. Search any of them by name to read them the same way.

steps.title: Your Workbench (demo)
steps.text: The tour signed you in as Demo analyst (no password; a made-up name keeps lists apart). The Workbench tracks your own IMM files and pinned decisions, and holds the document tools.

steps.title: A case list that flags change
steps.text: Paste IMM numbers, or a column from Excel, and the list follows those files. A flag shows when the stored Federal Court docket has moved since you last looked.

steps.title: Your pinned case
steps.text: Vavilov is here because the tour pinned it. Pins take folders and notes, and Compare selected sets two decisions side by side.

steps.title: Live document analysis
steps.text: Bring your own factum, memo or decision and read it the way the case reader shows a decision, with every citation and statute marked and checked against the library. It is read in memory, never stored, and no AI is used.

steps.title: A made-up Memorandum of Argument
steps.text: I pasted a fictional MOA from a cessation judicial review (nothing real). You could drop in a Word file or a text PDF instead.

steps.title: The document, marked up
steps.text: Read in markup mode. The bar counts the case citations and statute references found, and the layers can be switched on and off. Margin labels name each one.

steps.title: A case that is in the library
steps.text: This citation is matched to Vavilov in the library, with its pinpoint (paragraphs 10 and 99). Click it to open the decision at that paragraph.

steps.title: Short forms are followed too
steps.text: 'Vavilov, above at para 99' and 'Ibid at para 100' are traced back to the case they refer to, so a back-reference is not lost.

steps.title: Authorities the library does not hold
steps.text: Cases that are not in the library are still marked, so you can see which authorities cannot be checked here.

steps.title: Statute references
steps.text: Provisions of IRPA and the Federal Courts Act are found and tied to the statute library, including forms like 's. 25(1) of the IRPA'.

steps.title: The authority table
steps.text: One table of every authority in the document: how it was written, whether it is in the library, and how often it is mentioned. It downloads as a spreadsheet. I did not click 'Save library cases to Workbench'.

steps.title: De-identifier
steps.text: A separate tool in the Workbench: swap names, ID numbers, contact details and specific dates for placeholders such as [PERSON_1] before a document goes anywhere else. A key file puts them back. Nothing is stored.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.text: Search a judge to see their decisions in the library, how outcomes split, and which authorities they rely on. Name variants are merged so one judge is not split across spellings.

steps.title: One judge's record
steps.text: I opened the first judge in the list. A profile shows that judge's decisions, how they came out, and the authorities they cite.

steps.title: Citation intelligence
steps.text: Start from one authority and see who relies on it: which courts and judges cite it, the outcomes of the cases that cite it, the statutes they discuss, and how its use has changed year to year.

steps.title: Federal Court activity
steps.text: FC Analytics covers the classified Federal Court immigration docket: outcomes, timing, motions, judges and counsel, not only the files you received. Everything is read from the Court's registry entries for each file.

steps.title: Filters that every chart follows
steps.text: Years filed, registry, the decision under review (IRB divisions, visa offices, PRRA officers), application type, whether counsel is named, and language. Change one and the whole page re-draws.

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.text: The key numbers for whatever the filters select, at the top so you can see the size of the group before reading any rate.

steps.title: How files progress
steps.text: Files reaching each stage: leave decision, judicial review, judgment. The rest were discontinued, are still open, or ended another way.

steps.title: Grant rates by year filed
steps.text: The share of leave decisions, and of merits judgments, that were granted, year by year. Hover a point for the counts behind it.

steps.title: How each year's files ended
steps.text: Leave refused, discontinued, dismissed, granted, settled, still open. Click a year and the whole page filters to it.

steps.title: Leave rates by decision under review
steps.text: Bar length is the leave grant rate for challenges to each kind of decision (RPD, RAD, PRRA, visa offices and so on), with the number of files in brackets.

steps.title: Which office decided
steps.text: The most frequent visa posts, IRB regions and processing centres behind the decisions that reach the Court. Click one to filter.

steps.title: Time between steps
steps.text: Median days between filing, leave decision and judicial review, with the middle half of files shown as a band.

steps.title: Days from filing to leave decision
steps.text: Median days by year filed. Years with fewer than 30 leave decisions, often recent and still open, are left out so they do not mislead.

steps.title: Motions by type
steps.text: Ruled motions split granted and dismissed, plus withdrawn and never ruled. The grant rate counts ruled motions only.

steps.title: Judges: leave versus judicial review
steps.text: Each dot is a judge with at least 25 leave decisions: leave grant rate across, judicial review grant rate up, dot size by decisions. Click a dot to filter to that judge.

steps.title: Applicant counsel
steps.text: Counsel named on the applicant's side, with their files and rates. Click a row to see only their files.

steps.title: Procedural deadlines
steps.text: Whether the application was filed within the 15-day or 60-day limit in section 72 of IRPA, and the steps governed by Rules 10, 11 and 15.

steps.title: Why leave was refused
steps.text: Refusals where the applicant never filed a record, against refusals on the record. This separates abandoned files from files that lost.

steps.title: By registry
steps.text: Files by registry office with the leave grant rate. Click one to filter.

steps.title: Try a filter
steps.text: I chose Last 5 years. Every figure and chart above now covers only files filed in those years, and the chips under the filters show what is active so it can be removed.

steps.title: Read the rates with the caveats
steps.text: Rates use files with an observed decision, and counts sit beside every rate because small groups are not reliable. Motions never ruled on are inferred from what happened next, and Registry entries can contain errors.

steps.title: That is the tour
steps.text: You have seen search, the formatted reader, judges, citation intelligence, Federal Court analytics, the Workbench and the document tools. Take the tour again from the About page whenever you like. Press Done to explore on your own.
